Decision trees: models that ask questions

The most explainable model in ML, and the building block of the models that win on business data.

Press N for presenter lines · F fullscreen · arrows to move

The idea

Remember the game 20 Questions?

1 "Is it an animal?" splits the possibilities roughly in half
2 A good player asks the question that tells them the most first
3 A decision tree plays this game with customers: each question separates leavers from stayers

The tree our data actually learned (depth 2)

55.1% leave1,707 customers

How a tree gives a probability

Predict

drop the customer down the questions until they land in a box (a leaf)

Probability

share of leavers among the training customers in that leaf: 940 / 1,707 = 55%

Why? A tree says "customers like you left 55% of the time". Catch: every customer in one leaf gets the same score. Our best tree has 29 leaves, so only 29 different scores exist; many customers tie, which makes ranking coarse.

Why ask about the contract first?

Because it makes the boxes the most pure

Gini impurity = 1 − p² − (1−p)²
Why? p = share of leavers in a box. All stayers or all leavers → 0 (pure). A 50/50 box → 0.5 (worst). In plain words: pick two customers at random from the box; Gini is the chance they disagree.

Scoring the real first question

BoxCustomersLeaveGini
Before any question5,63426.5%0.390
Not month-to-month2,5326.7%0.125
Month-to-month3,10242.8%0.490
After the split (weighted by size)0.326
Why? Impurity fell 0.390 → 0.326. The tree tried every feature at every possible cut-point and this split gave the biggest drop. Then it repeats inside each box.

The algorithm (CART) is greedy

1 Find the single best question right now
2 Split, then repeat inside each box
3 Stop when a limit is hit (depth, leaf size) or a box is pure
Why? Why not search for the best whole tree? Finding the optimal tree is NP-complete (Hyafil & Rivest, 1976): impossible at scale. Greedy is fast but only locally best; a weak first question can never be undone.

Measuring impurity: all the options

CriterionIdeaOur CV AUC
Gini (default)chance two random customers disagree0.8328
Entropysurprise / information (from information theory, uses log)0.8325
Log losssame as entropy in scikit-learn0.8325
MSE / squared errorfor regression trees (predicting a number)n/a
Best choice: Gini. It gives the same trees in practice (difference 0.0003) and skips the logarithm, so it's slightly faster. Don't waste tuning time here; tune the size limits instead.

Leave a tree alone and it never stops

1,093 leaves · 24 questions deep · test AUC 0.665

Why? An unlimited tree keeps splitting until every box is pure, which means it memorises individual customers. Lesson 2 again: perfect on training data, poor on new customers. A limited tree with 29 leaves scores 0.833.

Four ways to stop a tree: tested on our data

Stopping rules: all the options

SettingWhat it meansBest on our dataNotes
max_depthat most N questions in a row5 → 0.829easiest to explain; but forces the same depth everywhere
min_samples_leafevery leaf holds ≥ N customers50 → 0.829also makes leaf probabilities trustworthy (no 1-customer leaves)
max_leaf_nodesat most N leaves; best splits first16 → 0.824grows where the data is rich
ccp_alpha (pruning)grow fully, then cut weak branches0.001 → 0.824principled, but alpha is hard to interpret
min_samples_split, max_featuresminor knobsrarely matter alonemax_features matters in random forests
Best choice: tune max_depth + min_samples_leaf together with cross-validation. Our grid search picked depth 5, ≥50 per leaf: CV 0.833, test 0.833, 29 leaves.

How does our best tree compare?

ModelTest AUCExplain to a manager?
Full tree (no limits)0.665no: 1,093 rules
Tuned tree (depth 5, ≥50 per leaf)0.833yes: 29 rules
Logistic regression (Lesson 4)0.842yes: one weight per feature
Why? The tree loses slightly. Why? Churn falls smoothly with tenure; a line captures that in one weight, a tree needs many steps to imitate it. Trees win when the pattern is "if this AND that" (interactions).

Predicting a number: a regression tree is a staircase

Why? Each leaf predicts the average of its customers; splits minimise squared error. Deeper = more steps. And beyond the training range it goes flat: a tree can never extrapolate.

Trees cut with straight walls only

Why? Every question is "feature ≤ value", so boundaries are made of horizontal and vertical walls. A diagonal pattern becomes a staircase.

The big weakness: trees are unstable

Why? We trained on 6 different halves of the data. The first question was always "month-to-month?", but deeper down the trees changed, and 26% of test customers got a different answer. Limits cut that to 6%. Small data changes → big model changes = high variance.

Which features matter? Two ways to ask the tree

Why? Impurity importance: how much each feature reduced Gini during training (free, instant). Permutation importance: shuffle one column on test data and measure how much AUC drops. Both agree: the contract dominates.

A trap almost everyone falls into

We added a column of pure random numbers

Why? Impurity importance ranked the random column #2! Why: a column with thousands of unique values offers thousands of cut-points, so a deep tree can always use it to memorise noise, and the score is computed on training data. Permutation on test data exposes it: shuffling noise changes nothing.

Feature importance: all the options

MethodHowStrengthWeakness
Impurity (built-in)sum of Gini drops in trainingfree, instantbiased toward many-valued features; training data only
Permutationshuffle a column, measure score drop on test datahonest, works for any modelcorrelated features hide each other; slower
SHAP valuesfair share of each feature per prediction (game theory)explains individual customersslower; more to explain
Drop-columnretrain without the featuremost directretrain per feature: expensive
Best choice: permutation importance on held-out data for "what matters overall"; SHAP when you must explain one customer's score. Never present impurity importance alone.

Decision trees: the honest scorecard

Strengths

• no scaling needed: a cut-point doesn't care about units
• mixes numbers & categories
• handles missing values (scikit-learn ≥ 1.3)
• readable rules
• fast to predict (just a few questions)

Weaknesses

• unstable (high variance)
• greedy: not globally best
• staircase boundaries
• cannot extrapolate
• coarse probabilities (one per leaf)

When should you use a single tree?

SituationUse
Explain the drivers to managers; make a simple rule card for staffshallow tree (depth 2–4)
Smooth effects, need calibrated probabilities, small datalogistic regression
Maximum accuracy on business (tabular) dataensembles of trees: random forest, gradient boosting (next lesson)
Images, text, audioneural networks (Part II)
Best choice: a single tree is a superb explainer, rarely the final production model. Its real job is being the brick that forests and boosting are built from.

Say this in an interview

Q "How does a tree choose a split?" → tries every feature & cut-point, picks the largest weighted drop in Gini; greedy, because optimal trees are NP-complete
Q "Why do trees overfit?" → unlimited, they split until every leaf is pure; control with depth / leaf size tuned by CV
Q "Can you trust feature_importances_?" → no, it's biased to high-cardinality features; use permutation or SHAP on held-out data

Bridge to modern AI

In the age of LLMs, trees still rule tables

1 On tabular data, tree ensembles still usually beat deep learning (Grinsztajn et al., NeurIPS 2022)
2 In Part II, our AI agent will call a churn model as a tool, and explain its answer with SHAP
3 The idea of routing an input down a path returns in "mixture of experts" LLMs, which send each word to a few expert sub-networks

Check yourself · 1 of 5

A leaf holds 200 customers; 50 left. What probability does a new customer landing there get?

Answer25% (50 / 200). Every customer in that leaf gets the same score.

Check yourself · 2 of 5

A box is 50% leavers. Another is 10% leavers. Which has the higher Gini impurity?

AnswerThe 50% box: Gini 0.5 (maximum). The 10% box: 1 − 0.01 − 0.81 = 0.18.

Check yourself · 3 of 5

Your unlimited tree scores 99.8% on training data and AUC 0.66 on test. Name two fixes.

AnswerLimit it: max_depth and/or min_samples_leaf, tuned with cross-validation (or prune with ccp_alpha).

Check yourself · 4 of 5

Do you need to scale features before training a decision tree? Why?

AnswerNo. A split only asks "is it above this value?", which works the same in any units.

Check yourself · 5 of 5

A random ID column is a top feature in feature_importances_. Why, and what do you do?

AnswerImpurity importance is biased toward many-valued columns and measured on training data. Use permutation importance on test data; it will rank the ID near zero.
RememberA tree asks the question that makes boxes purest.
Stop it early, or it memorises.
Great explainer, unstable alone.
